title: SQLite: Your First Database
summary: See why a CSV file alone is not enough, then design the quotes table (schema.sql) and create market.db with the standard-library module sqlite3. Learn by running it: the connect, execute, commit, close order; inserting safely with ? placeholders and executemany; constraints rejecting bad rows; asking questions with SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT; and SQL injection.

create_db.summary: Create the table with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS from schema.sql, insert the five rows of prices.csv in one go with a seven-? INSERT and executemany, then commit. It is safe to run again (it deletes and reloads). Then observe, in turn, the limits of file storage, what happens when you forget commit, and constraint violations.
create_db.notes: The slides' cd 13week/examples/sqlite_lab is ~/week13/examples/sqlite_lab in this lab. market.db is a result that can be rebuilt, so it is not submitted (*.db in .gitignore).
steps: sqlite3 is part of the standard library, so there is nothing to install. No server, no login: one file is the whole database. This virtual machine has no sqlite3 command-line shell, so all SQL is run from Python.
What a CSV cannot do: every question means reading all the rows and looping (5 3). Even prices arrive as <class 'str'>. Nothing stops a duplicate row or a missing price.

Two users, one file: both read 100 before the other saves, and each saves 50. saved: 50 expected: 0. One withdrawal disappears without any error (a lost update). A file cannot make writers take turns.

Seven columns and their types: date, code, name and market are TEXT; prices in KRW and volume are INTEGER. code must be TEXT so that 005930 does not become 5930. NOT NULL, CHECK (prices > 0, volume >= 0) and PRIMARY KEY (date, code) are the rules the table enforces. code alone cannot be the key, because tomorrow's price for the same stock will arrive too.
market.db ready: 5 rows. connect("market.db") created a file that did not exist. A database, too, is in the end an ordinary file on disk.
The second run does not fail either, and it is still 5 rows. IF NOT EXISTS leaves the existing table alone, and DELETE FROM quotes empties it before inserting again.
Every value read from the CSV was a string, but the INTEGER column stored "71400" as the number 71400 (integer), and the TEXT column stored '005930' exactly as written.

Forget commit() and the row is lost. Within the same connection it shows (6,), but after closing without commit and reopening it is (5,). No error, no warning. "It worked on my screen" is not "it was saved".

A script that previews Lab C. Inserting the existing (2026-11-05, 000660) again gives IntegrityError UNIQUE constraint failed: quotes.date, quotes.code; changing close to 0 gives IntegrityError CHECK constraint failed: close > 0. Only the failed statement is cancelled, and the row count stays (5,).

queries.summary: The starter file for the five-questions lab. Only Q1 (names and closing prices of KOSPI stocks, ordered by code) is written; Q2 to Q5 are only questions in comments. Run the SELECT examples from the slides to gather what you need for Q2 to Q5. Every value from outside goes in through a ? placeholder.
queries.notes: Write Q2 to Q5 yourself with nano queries.py and check them with python3 queries.py. Q5 reads a code with input(), so you can also test it by piping input, as in printf '005930\n' | python3 queries.py. A one-value tuple such as (code,) needs the comma.
steps: Under Q1 KOSPI stocks you get ('SK하이닉스', 198000), ('삼성전자', 71400), ('NAVER', 200000). The order is not by name but ORDER BY code (000660, 005930, 035420). "KOSPI" is passed not inside the SQL string but as the tuple ("KOSPI",).
SELECT picks the columns. Each row comes back as one tuple in the order of the columns you asked for. Without ORDER BY, no order is promised (right now it just happens to look like insertion order).

WHERE picks the rows. = compares, and AND combines conditions. The only result is [('에코프로비엠', 103000)]. JYP Ent. is also on KOSDAQ, but its close of 49000 is less than 50000. close is INTEGER, so the comparison is numeric.

ORDER BY volume DESC sorts largest first and LIMIT 3 keeps only the first three rows: 삼성전자 1000000, SK하이닉스 500000, NAVER 300000. If there are ties, give a second sort column, as in ORDER BY volume DESC, code.

Inside SELECT, compute the same formula as change_pct() in logic.py, name it with AS and use it in ORDER BY. The output runs from +3.0% 에코프로비엠 to -2.0% JYP Ent. Each row is unpacked into two variables, name and pct.

Trap: in SQL, integer / integer drops the decimals. 7 / 2 is 3, 7 * 1.0 / 2 is 3.5, and (71400 - 70000) / 70000, without multiplying by 100.0 first, becomes 0. ":memory:" is a temporary database with no file.

SQL injection: an f-string pastes the input into the SQL text, so the quote inside the input rewrites the condition into OR '1'='1'. Reading the printed SQL shows why you get (5,), that is, every row. With ?, the input is only ever a value, and there is no market with that name, so the result is (0,).

With sqlite3.Row you get values by column name, as in row["close"] instead of row[2]. You get 삼성전자 71400, and in dict(row) the price is already <class 'int'> while the code stays 005930. This dict is exactly the shape logic.py expects (Session 2).
